title: Patrick
hook: a British boy kidnapped to Ireland escapes, then goes back to the people who enslaved him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chalcedon, and one person in two natures. Your line was truly god, truly human.

Raiders come to a family's land in Britain and carry off a boy, along with many others, across the sea to Ireland. He's put to work watching animals on the hills, alone. His father was a deacon, his grandfather a priest, and the boy, by his own account, had paid none of it much attention. Now, out on the hillside, he starts to pray. Years later he'll write the story himself, in rough Latin he apologizes for.

Patrick's Confession doesn't read like a legend. It reads like a man explaining his life to people who doubted him. On that hillside, he says, the love of God grew in him. He prayed day and night, in snow and frost and rain, and felt no harm. Then one night he heard a voice in his sleep: your ship is ready. He ran a long way to a coast he didn't know, talked his way onto a ship, and after hard days, and some years, was home with his family. They begged him never to leave again. Then came another dream. A man named Victoricus seemed to come from Ireland, carrying letters, more than could be counted. He handed one over, and at the top it said: The Voice of the Irish. As he read, he heard the people beside the western sea calling, as if with one voice: holy boy, we beg you, come and walk among us again. And he went back. To the land where he'd been a slave, to the people who had taken him. As a bishop he baptized and ordained, and refused gifts, even handing back what was left on the altar, so no one could say he'd come for profit. It wasn't safe: he writes of being seized and put in chains. Jesus had said, in the King James: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you." Patrick doesn't cast himself as the hero. He calls himself a sinner, the least of the faithful, and gives the credit to God. The shamrock and the snakes come from later stories. His own pages hold something stranger: a man who went back.
screen: `BACK TO THE PEOPLE WHO TOOK HIM.`
`NO SHAMROCK: A MAN WHO WENT BACK.`

segments.voice: Let a place or person tied to an old hurt come to mind, not the deepest, something you can hold today; going back in your heart never means walking back into harm. Is there a good thing you could bring there now, a kind word, or simply wishing them well from a distance? If you pray, bring that place to God; if not, hold it in steady goodwill.
Patrick. The captive who escaped, then heard the voice of the Irish and went back. That ends a week of Jerome, the pears, Ostia, Rome, the golden mouth and Chalcedon.
Your line: the voice of the irish. He went back, carrying something good. A week done.

howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox and other Christians honor Patrick as a saint and the apostle of Ireland; his Confession is read as his own account of his captivity, escape and return.

chat.says: What's so surprising about Patrick's story, if you read what he actually wrote?
options: He escaped slavery in Ireland, then chose to go back to the people who took him.
He was born in Ireland and never left, preaching to his own neighbors all his life.
He came as a rich noble, and the Irish kings paid him well to preach.
chat.meaning: In his own Confession, Patrick, once a captive, heard the voice of the Irish and went back to the land where he'd been a slave.

notes: No age or numbers stated (Confession 1 gives 'about sixteen' and 'many thousands'; the script says 'along with many others'). Father Calpornius a deacon, grandfather Potitus a priest (Confession 1); names omitted. Confirm.
Confession 16–17: prayer on the hills in snow, frost and rain; the voice 'your ship is ready'; the long flight to the coast. Paraphrased.

Confession 23: Victoricus, 'innumerable letters', 'Vox Hiberionacum', the voices by the wood of Foclut near the western sea: 'we ask thee, holy youth, to come and walk among us once more'. Paraphrased; please confirm the Latin spelling and pronunciation in the original game.
Confession 49–52: returning gifts left on the altar; being seized and put in irons. Confirm.
Shamrock and snakes: from later hagiography and folklore, not in the Confession. Week-end look-back in the word segment covers days 778–784.
